about.dates: This report covers your session on Tuesday 20 October 2026 and was prepared on 20 October 2026. If a session is re-analysed, the report is prepared again and carries the new date.
about.footnote: Measured and prepared with PinPoint Studio. Swing images show only the golfer; video stays in the studio.
about.measured: 19 swings with a 7 iron and gap wedge, filmed face-on at high frame rate, with seven of the balls measured by a GC Quad. Your body positions are read from the video by pose tracking; the club and ball numbers come from the launch monitor.
about.notChecked: Some things could not be checked on every swing. How fast the club was moving at its peak: our cameras could see it, but not well enough to judge (19 of 19 swings). Hip turn at the top: a single face-on camera cannot measure how far you turn; a down-the-line camera or a body sensor can (19 of 19 swings). Chest turn at the finish: a single face-on camera cannot measure how far you turn; a down-the-line camera or a body sensor can (19 of 19 swings). When your hips turned fastest: the face-on camera cannot time a turn while you are square to it; a down-the-line camera or a body sensor can (18 of 19 swings). Two more are listed in the technical appendix. Where that touches one of your work-ons, its page says so.
about.ranges: Each habit is judged against a target range. Most ranges are coaching judgement, set from what good ball-strikers do; a few come from published measurements. They are not fitted to you. A swing outside the range is not a mistake in itself — it is where the evidence points. “Ruled out” on a work-on page means measured, and fine, on these swings with these cameras — not gone for good.

consistency.key: A cell takes the grade of the third of its readings that move most: %1, %2, %3, %4 or %5, from least movement to most. %6: fewer than eight swings to grade it. %7: it moves no more than the reading's own measurement error. workOns.check: Film face-on. At the top your head and chest should sit a little behind the ball, never toward the target.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Reverse spine angle at P4, or “leaning left at the top”, “forward spine angle at the top”.
workOns.cue: At the top, feel your breastbone stay over your trail thigh.

drills.equipment: a mirror, or a phone on a stand
drills.instruction: Without a ball, hold a club across your chest. Turn to the top and check in a mirror, or on a phone face-on, that your head and chest sit a little behind the ball, with your upper body tilted slightly away from the target. Make ten slow turns.
drills.label: Club across the chest
drills.note: A short turn often hides inside this one: if the shoulders cannot turn further, the body tips instead, and a physical check of your upper back comes first.
drills.targets: To feel your upper body staying behind the ball as it turns, rather than tipping toward the target or hanging too far back.

workOns.goal: Lean slightly away from the target at the top
workOns.kicker: Work-on 1 of 3  ·  P4, at the top  ·  19 of 19 swings
workOns.name: Reverse spine angle at P4
workOns.saw: You lean toward the target at the top — on all 19 swings, no change from first swing to last. Typical lean away from the target at the top: 12° the other way (you lean more toward the target at the top), against a target of 0° or more; this is a clear miss: well past the range on 18 of 19 swings.
workOns.target: Lean away from the target at the top: 0° or more, on most swings. Today: 12° the other way (you lean more toward the target at the top).
workOns.why: Leaning toward the target at the top strains your lower back and makes it hard to start down smoothly.

workOns.cameWith: The coaching model says it can bring other habits with it. Not today — on every swing, you keep the wrist angle starting down.

workOns.check: Film face-on. Halfway down, your hands should still be in front of the middle of your chest, with your chest already turning toward the ball.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Arms outrun the chest, or “arms first”, “arms take over”.
workOns.cue: Feel your arms and the club stay in front of your chest as it turns, as if your chest were carrying them down.

drills.instruction: Tuck a small towel under your lead upper arm and make three-quarter swings without dropping it.
drills.label: Towel under the lead arm
drills.note: Easy to overdo. The arm should stay connected, not pinned — a swing with no separation at all is its own fault.
drills.targets: To feel the lead arm and the chest moving as one unit through the backswing.

drills.instruction: Make swings with a one-second pause at the top. From the pause, start down with your lower body, letting your weight move toward your lead foot while your chest stays behind the ball for a moment. Start with half swings and short irons.
drills.label: Pause at the top
drills.note: The pause is a rehearsal, not a new swing. Once the order feels natural, let the pause shrink until it has gone.
drills.targets: To give your lower body time to start the downswing, so your upper body is not rushed toward the ball.

workOns.goal: Turn your chest and let your arms follow
workOns.kicker: Work-on 2 of 3  ·  P7, at impact  ·  18 of 18 swings
workOns.name: Arms outrun the chest
workOns.saw: Your arms race ahead of your chest coming down — on all 18 swings, no change from first swing to last. It could not be measured on 1 of 19 swings: we could not pin down its timing closely enough to compare it with the rest.
workOns.why: When your arms take over before your chest has turned, the speed your body made is left behind and your arms have to make it alone.

workOns.cameWith: The coaching model says it can bring other habits with it. Not today — on every swing we could see, your strikes stay near the middle of the face.

workOns.check: Film face-on and hold the finish until the ball lands. Your hips should be stacked over your lead foot, and you should be able to stand there without stepping.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Cannot hold the finish, or “falling over”, “stepping through”.

workOns.cue: Feel yourself swing to a tall finish with your weight on your lead heel and your trail toe just resting on the ground.

drills.instruction: Hit the shot and hold your finish, balanced on the lead foot, until the ball lands. If you cannot hold it, take 20 yards off the swing and try again.
drills.label: Hold the finish
drills.note: The most diagnostic drill in this list: where you fall tells you what happened earlier.
drills.targets: To make balance the constraint the swing is built inside, rather than something checked afterwards.

drills.instruction: Stand with your feet together and hit easy half to three-quarter shots off a low tee. Let your arms swing and your body turn only as fast as you can stay balanced, and hold the finish each time.
drills.label: Feet-together swings
drills.note: Short shots only. If you cannot stay balanced even at half speed, balance on one leg is worth checking before anything else.
drills.targets: To feel the arms, body and club working together at a speed your balance can support, rather than the body lunging or the arms going on their own.

workOns.why: A finish you can't hold shows your swing was off balance earlier, so your shots are hard to repeat.
